title: Gregory the Great
hook: a pope who called himself servant of the servants of God

segments.voice: Yesterday, Columba, the pilgrim for Christ. Your line was the island mission. Where was your quiet place? Day seven hundred eighty-nine.

Old letters open with a name and a title. Dear Sir. From the Office of the Director. Titles tell you where someone stands. Two days ago, we heard the story of Scholastica's storm. The man who wrote it down was a bishop of Rome, a pope, and he signed his letters with a title of his own choosing. Not lord of the church. Not head of anything. He called himself servant of the servants of God. Today, the man who picked it, and why it was harder to live than to write.

His name was Gregory, and later Christians called him the Great. Before he was pope, he had been a monk. He had turned his family's house in Rome into a monastery, and he loved the quiet there. Then he was made bishop of Rome, and the quiet ended. Bede, writing about him later, passes on Gregory's own complaint: that the cares of his office pulled his mind away from prayer, like a ship tossed in a storm, looking back at the shore it had left. So he knew what the job could do to a person. He wrote a whole book about it, the Pastoral Rule, a guide for anyone who leads souls. One of its warnings is that the person at the top is in special danger of pride. And the title. Servus servorum Dei, servant of the servants of God. It echoes something Jesus said to his friends when two of them asked for the places of honor beside him. In Mark's Gospel he tells them, "whosoever of you will be the chiefest, shall be servant of all." Gregory took that and put it at the top of his letters, where everyone would see it, including him. Christians remember him differently depending on where they stand. Catholics count him among the great popes and teachers of the church. Orthodox Christians honor him too, as Saint Gregory the Dialogist, after the book where Benedict's story is told. And a thread for tomorrow: Gregory is the one who sent monks to England. A title is a promise you make in public. His said: I'm here to serve those who serve God.

Here's the practice: serve someone whose work usually goes unseen. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the people who make your day work and rarely get thanked. The person who cleans the building. The one who drives the bus, answers the phones, stocks the shelves, empties the bins. Pick one. Think about what their day might be like. Then choose one small way to serve them back: learn their name, say thank you properly, make their job easier by a minute. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, just hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Gregory. The monk who became pope, later called the Great, and signed himself servant of the servants of God.
Your line: servant of servants. Today, do the small thing you chose for the person you named, without being asked and without telling anyone. Day seven hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics honor Gregory the Great as a pope and Doctor of the Church, and Orthodox Christians honor him as Saint Gregory the Dialogist; the plainchant called Gregorian chant is named after him by tradition.

fork.setup: you're a monk who loves the quiet of the monastery. you're made bishop of Rome, and the quiet is over. what do you do?
options: refuse and stay in the monastery.
take it, and choose a title that keeps you low.
take it, and leave the monastery behind for good.
fork.reveal: Gregory took up the office, grieved the lost quiet, and signed himself servant of the servants of God.

original.note: Latin: servant of the servants of God, the title Gregory used in his letters.

what it means: a monk who became pope and called himself the servant of servants, after Jesus's words in Mark.
what a scholar hears: servus servorum Dei, a title at the head of his letters, and the Pastoral Rule's warning that leaders are at special risk of pride.

notes: Bede 2.1 passes on Gregory's lament (from the preface to the Dialogues) comparing himself to a ship tossed by waves; paraphrased. Confirm.
Gregory turned his family home on the Caelian Hill into a monastery (St Andrew's): confirm via Bede 2.1.
Cut per the claims rule: that later popes kept 'servus servorum Dei' on their documents. A Keeper may restore it with a source.
Pastoral Rule's repeated warning about the ruler's pride: paraphrased summary; confirm.
Orthodox title 'the Dialogist' (Dvoeslov) and Catholic 'Doctor of the Church': confirm. howItsDone's Gregorian chant line is attributed to tradition; confirm.
The hook says the man who wrote down Scholastica's story was pope; Gregory wrote the Dialogues as pope. Confirm.

Editor: Mark 10:44 context corrected (James and John asking for places of honor, not the 'who is greatest' argument of Mark 9); Pastoral Rule claim softened from 'over and over / most in danger'; 'every letter' and 'busiest job' cut; 'lovely' cut.
Editor (second pass): review line no longer says Columba 'never went home' (Adomnán records later visits to Ireland).

Audit: closing gloss of the title corrected from 'the people who serve' to 'those who serve God', matching servus servorum Dei. Keeper may add that Gregory tried to avoid election (Gregory of Tours, History 10.1); the fork currently does not say so.
